blocks.text: Rabin Karp is a string matching algorithm that finds every occurrence of a pattern inside a text using a technique called a rolling hash, instead of comparing characters one by one at every starting position.

Instead of asking "do these two strings match character by character" at every single window, Rabin Karp first asks a much cheaper question: "do these two windows even hash to the same value" . Only when the answer is yes does it bother checking characters.

With careful use of a rolling hash, Rabin Karp can search for a pattern of length m inside a text of length n in O(n+m) average time, the same asymptotic bound as far more intricate algorithms like KMP, while using an idea that is genuinely simple to implement from scratch.

items: Naive matching: compares the pattern against the text at every position, character by character
Rabin Karp: compares cheap hash values first, and only falls back to character comparison when the hashes agree

blocks.text: This makes Rabin Karp one of the few string matching algorithms that generalizes naturally to searching for multiple patterns at once, which is exactly where it shines in practice.

content.title: 1. The Problem with Naive String Matching

blocks.text: The most direct way to find a pattern inside a text is to try every possible starting position and check, character by character, whether the pattern matches there.
For a text of length n and a pattern of length m, there are roughly n-m+1 starting positions to try, and each one can take up to m character comparisons before a mismatch is found.

In the worst case, such as searching for a pattern of a thousand as followed by a b inside a text made almost entirely of the letter a, nearly every starting position matches for a long stretch before the final character reveals a mismatch. This pushes naive matching to O(n*m) time.

A text of a million as and a pattern of a thousand as followed by a b forces naive matching to redo almost the entire comparison at every single position, roughly a billion character comparisons for a search that feels like it should be fast.

Rabin Karp fixes this without abandoning the simple sliding window idea. It keeps the same window sliding across the text, but replaces the expensive per-position character comparison with something that can be checked in O(1): a hash value.

content.title: 2. The Core Idea: Hash First, Verify Second

blocks.text: The key insight behind Rabin Karp is that comparing two strings for equality can be approximated by comparing two numbers.

If every string is assigned a numeric hash value, then two equal strings are guaranteed to produce the same hash. So instead of comparing the pattern to the text window character by character, Rabin Karp compares:

items: hash(pattern), computed once, before the search begins
hash(text[i..i+m-1]), the hash of the current window, recomputed as the window slides

blocks.text: If the two hashes differ, the strings are definitely different, no character comparison is needed at all, and the window slides forward immediately.

If the two hashes are equal, the strings are probably equal, but not certainly, since different strings can occasionally produce the same hash value. Only in this case does Rabin Karp fall back to a real character by character comparison to confirm an actual match.
This is the entire algorithm in one sentence: hash the pattern once, hash every window of the text, compare hashes, and only compare characters when the hashes agree.

This is exactly why Rabin Karp's average case performance beats naive matching. Most windows have a completely different hash from the pattern, so most windows are rejected in O(1) with no character comparison at all.

content.title: 3. The Rolling Hash: O(1) Window Updates

blocks.text: There is one problem left to solve. If computing the hash of a window of length m takes O(m) time by itself, then recomputing it for every one of the n-m+1 windows would cost O(n*m) overall, the same as naive matching, defeating the entire purpose of hashing.
The fix is the rolling hash: a way to compute the hash of the next window in O(1), by reusing the hash of the current window instead of recomputing it from scratch.
Treating a string as a number
A string is treated as a number written in some base b, the same way the digits 3, 1, 4 represent the number three hundred and fourteen in base 10.
For a string s of length m, its hash under base b is:
where each s[i] is the numeric value of that character, such as its ASCII code.

Now consider sliding the window forward by one position, from text[i..i+m-1] to text[i+1..i+m]. The new window shares m-1 characters with the old one. Only the leading character text[i] leaves, and one new trailing character text[i+m] enters.
This means the new hash can be built directly from the old hash in three arithmetic steps:

items: Remove the leading character's contribution: subtract text[i] * b^(m-1)
Shift every remaining place value up by one: multiply the result by b
Add the new trailing character: add text[i+m]

blocks.text: Every one of these three steps is O(1), so sliding the window across the entire text costs O(n) total instead of O(n*m). This single formula is the entire reason Rabin Karp beats naive matching: it reuses work instead of throwing it away at every step.

content.title: 4. Worked Example: Rolling the Hash by Hand

blocks.text: Here is the rolling hash formula applied to real numbers, so the arithmetic is visible end to end.
Take the text "ababab" and the pattern "aba" (so m = 3). Use the mapping a = 1, b = 2, base 31, and modulus 101 (the choice of modulus is explained in the next section).
First, hash the pattern "aba" directly:

So hash(pattern) = 14. The first window of the text, text[0..2] = "aba", is the identical substring, so it hashes to the same value, an immediate hash match, and since the strings really are identical, verification confirms a real occurrence at index 0.

Now slide the window forward by one, to text[1..3] = "bab". Instead of recomputing from scratch, roll the hash: remove the contribution of the leading character text[0] = 'a' = 1, shift, and add the new trailing character text[3] = 'b' = 2.

codes.javascript:
b^(m-1) mod q = 31^2 mod 101 = 961 mod 101 = 52

remove leading 'a':  (14 - 1*52 + 101) mod 101 = 63
shift by base:       (63 * 31) mod 101 = 34
add trailing 'b':    (34 + 2) mod 101 = 36

newHash = 36

blocks.text: That matches a direct computation of hash("bab") mod 101 = 36. Since 36 is not 14, this window is rejected instantly, no character comparison needed.

Rolling forward once more to text[2..4] = "aba" (removing text[1] = 'b' = 2, adding text[4] = 'a' = 1) brings the rolling hash back to 14, correctly flagging another hash match, which verification confirms as a real occurrence of "aba" at index 2.
Every rolling step used only a handful of additions, subtractions, and multiplications, never a full rescan of the window. That is the O(1) update in action.
The raw formula hash(s) = s[0]*b^(m-1) + ... + s[m-1] grows exponentially with string length. For even a moderately long pattern, b^m overflows a 64 bit integer almost immediately.
To keep numbers bounded, every hash computation is done modulo a large value q:

A common practical choice is a large prime such as 1000000007, paired with a base like 256 (treating characters as raw byte values) or a smaller base like 31 for lowercase letters. Using a prime modulus spreads hash values evenly and reduces the chance that unrelated strings collide.
Why collisions happen

A modulus shrinks a huge space of possible string values down into a much smaller range of remainders. By the pigeonhole principle, many different strings are guaranteed to map to the same hash value eventually, these are called collisions.
Collisions are not just a theoretical concern with weak hash functions. Consider a naive hash that simply sums character codes and ignores position entirely:

Two completely different strings, "ab" and "ba", produce the exact same hash, because plain addition does not care about order. This is why Rabin Karp's hash multiplies by increasing powers of the base at each position, giving earlier characters more weight than later ones, which makes collisions far less frequent, though it cannot make them impossible.

A hash match is a candidate, never a proof. Rabin Karp always performs a real character by character comparison before reporting a match, precisely because a fixed modulus makes rare collisions mathematically inevitable.

blocks.caption: A hash match is only a candidate. Verification either confirms a real occurrence or catches a collision.

blocks.text: Putting the pattern hash, the rolling window hash, and the verification step together gives the complete algorithm.
highOrder precomputes b^(m-1) mod q once, since that exact value is needed on every roll to remove the leading character's contribution.
The initial patternHash and windowHash are both built the same way, character by character, using the standard hash = hash*b + nextChar update.
Inside the main loop, a hash match triggers text.compare(i, m, pattern), a direct character comparison, before the index is ever accepted as a real match.
After checking position i, the window rolls forward using the same three step update derived earlier: remove, shift, add.

blocks.text: The worst case for Rabin Karp happens when the hash function collides on almost every window, forcing a full O(m) character verification at every position and degrading performance to the same O(n*m) bound as naive matching. With a good base and a large prime modulus, this is rare in practice, expected performance stays at O(n+m).

This worst case guarantee is weaker than KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt), which achieves a guaranteed O(n+m) even in the worst case by using a precomputed failure function instead of hashing. Rabin Karp trades that guarantee for a much simpler implementation and, crucially, the ability to search for many patterns at once.

content.title: 8. Multiple Pattern Matching and Duplicate Substrings

blocks.text: Naive matching and KMP are both built around searching for a single pattern. Extending them to search for many patterns at once usually means running the whole algorithm once per pattern.
Rabin Karp generalizes far more naturally, because a hash is just a number, and numbers are trivial to store in a set or a map.

To search for k patterns of the same length m at once, hash every pattern into a map from hash value to pattern index, then slide a single rolling window across the text exactly once, checking the map at every step:

This runs in roughly O(n + total pattern length) average time, regardless of how many patterns there are, because the text itself is scanned only once. Naive matching would need O(n*m) time per pattern, repeated k times.
Detecting duplicate substrings

The same rolling hash idea underlies algorithms for finding duplicate substrings of a fixed length inside a single string: hash every window of that length using a rolling hash, and store each hash in a set. If a hash is seen twice, verify the two windows character by character to confirm a true duplicate rather than a collision.

This is exactly the technique behind problems like Longest Duplicate Substring, typically combined with binary search on the candidate length, using Rabin Karp's rolling hash to check each candidate length in O(n) average time.
Common mistakes

items: Choosing a small or weak modulus: a small prime or a power of two makes collisions frequent, so nearly every window ends up needing a full character verification, degrading performance toward O(n*m).
Forgetting to verify after a hash match: trusting the hash blindly turns rare but real collisions into silently wrong answers.
Never taking the modulus: letting b^m grow unchecked overflows even a 64 bit integer for moderately long patterns.
Recomputing the window hash from scratch on every slide: this quietly turns an O(n+m) algorithm back into an O(n*m) one, skipping the entire point of rolling.

Getting the subtraction sign wrong: subtracting the leading character's contribution without adding the modulus back before the next mod operation can produce a negative hash, since the modulo of a negative number is itself negative in languages like C++.

blocks.text: Problem patterns

items: Medium Repeated String Match (LC 686): find the minimum number of times a string must be repeated so another string becomes a substring of it
Easy Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String (LC 28): the canonical single pattern search problem
Hard Longest Duplicate Substring (LC 1044): binary search on length combined with a rolling hash to detect duplicates
Medium Shortest Palindrome (LC 214): a rolling hash compares a prefix against its reverse in O(1) per check
Medium Distinct Echo Substrings: counts substrings formed by a string concatenated with itself, where a rolling hash keeps each equality check O(1) average

blocks.text: Rabin Karp is not always the fastest string matching algorithm on paper, but it is one of the most practical: simple to implement from scratch, easy to extend to multiple patterns, and a foundational building block behind duplicate substring and rolling hash problems across interviews and competitive programming.
